title: Indwelling Urinary Catheters: Need Is the First Safety Check
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: An indwelling urinary catheter should remain only when a valid indication exists. Convenience or routine incontinence care is not an appropriate reason for continued catheter exposure.
recognize: Acute retention, selected perioperative needs, critical output monitoring, prolonged immobilization, selected wound-healing situations, or end-of-life comfort may justify use depending on context.
priorities: Verify the current indication and escalate when the catheter no longer appears necessary.
assessMonitor: Review indication, duration, mobility, continence options, urinary retention risk, and output needs.
interventions: Use alternatives such as toileting plans, external devices, bladder scanning, or intermittent catheterization when clinically appropriate and ordered/policy-supported.
medicationSafety: Do not use antimicrobials simply because a catheter is present.
teaching: Explain that removing an unnecessary catheter reduces infection and injury risk.
delegationScope: Daily indication review requires licensed nursing/medical oversight; routine care may be delegated.
examTrap: Keeping a catheter because the patient is incontinent and staff are busy.
oneLinePearl: Every catheter day needs a reason.

title: Closed Urinary Drainage: Keep the System Sealed and Flowing
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: CAUTI prevention depends on a closed drainage system with unobstructed flow and the collection bag positioned below bladder level without resting on the floor.
recognize: Disconnected tubing, dependent loops, kinks, overfilled bags, or a bag above bladder level increase contamination/backflow risk.
priorities: Restore unobstructed dependent drainage and maintain the closed system.
assessMonitor: Inspect tubing, securement, bag position, urine flow, leakage, and system connections.
interventions: Empty the bag using clean technique and avoid unnecessary disconnections.
medicationSafety: Do not instill antiseptic or antimicrobial solutions into the drainage bag routinely.
teaching: At home, keep tubing unkinked and the bag below bladder level.
delegationScope: Routine drainage care may be delegated to trained staff; system compromise requires licensed review.
examTrap: Placing the urine bag on the bed beside the patient.
oneLinePearl: Closed, below the bladder, and unobstructed.

title: Catheter Obstruction: No Urine Plus Pain Needs Evaluation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Falling or absent catheter output with suprapubic discomfort, bladder distention, leakage around the catheter, clots, or acute kidney-risk cues may indicate obstruction. Check the system and escalate rather than assuming low urine production.
recognize: Kinks, dependent loops, sediment, clots, catheter migration, or true oliguria can all reduce drainage.
priorities: Inspect tubing/bag position, assess bladder distention and patient status, and report unresolved obstruction.
assessMonitor: Trend urine output, bladder symptoms, renal function as ordered, hydration, and catheter patency.
interventions: Reposition tubing and follow prescribed obstruction/irrigation protocol only when indicated.
medicationSafety: Routine bladder irrigation is not recommended without a clinical indication/order.
teaching: Home patients should report sudden output loss, pain, or leakage around the catheter.
delegationScope: Output measurement may be delegated; troubleshooting obstruction requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Documenting zero urine as oliguria before checking for a kinked catheter.
oneLinePearl: No catheter output can be kidney failure—or a blocked tube; check both.

title: Urinary Retention: Bladder Scan Before Unnecessary Catheterization
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Inability to void, small frequent voids, suprapubic fullness, agitation, or overflow leakage can signal retention. Use the facility bladder-scan/retention pathway when appropriate instead of reflexively inserting an indwelling catheter.
recognize: Postoperative status, opioids, anticholinergics, neurologic disease, obstruction, and immobility raise retention risk.
priorities: Assess symptoms, voiding pattern, medication contributors, and bladder volume using trained scanning when indicated.
assessMonitor: Trend voids, scan findings, intake/output, pain, and renal status.
interventions: Use toileting, mobility, privacy, intermittent catheterization, or other ordered measures based on protocol.
medicationSafety: Review medications that can worsen retention; do not independently stop them without clinical direction.
teaching: Report inability to void with increasing discomfort promptly.
delegationScope: Bladder scanning requires training; interpretation/escalation remains licensed responsibility.
examTrap: Placing a Foley immediately for every postoperative patient who has not yet voided.
oneLinePearl: Measure retention before creating catheter risk when the situation allows.

title: Intermittent Catheterization: Empty on Schedule, Protect the Urethra
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Intermittent catheterization can reduce prolonged indwelling-catheter exposure in selected bladder-emptying problems. It must follow the prescribed schedule/technique to prevent overdistention, trauma, and infection.
recognize: Large residuals, missed catheterizations, resistance, pain, or bleeding require review.
priorities: Use the prescribed clean/aseptic technique for the setting and maintain the scheduled emptying plan.
assessMonitor: Track catheterized volumes, voiding pattern, urethral trauma, symptoms of infection, and hydration.
interventions: Use adequate lubrication and gentle technique; never force against resistance.
medicationSafety: Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not automatically indicated solely because intermittent catheterization is used.
teaching: Home patients should demonstrate technique and know when to seek help.
delegationScope: Authority varies by setting and patient population; competency validation is required.
examTrap: Forcing the catheter when resistance is met.
oneLinePearl: Scheduled emptying, gentle technique, no forcing.

title: Suprapubic Catheter: Site and Drainage Both Need Surveillance
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A suprapubic catheter still carries infection, blockage, leakage, and dislodgement risk. Monitor both the abdominal insertion site and urinary drainage system.
recognize: Reduced drainage, bladder spasms, leakage, fever, site erythema/purulence, or tube displacement are concerning.
priorities: Maintain dependent closed drainage, inspect securement/site, and escalate obstruction or dislodgement.
assessMonitor: Trend urine output, site appearance, pain/spasms, temperature, and catheter position.
interventions: Use prescribed site care and flushing only when ordered.
medicationSafety: Antispasmodics or antibiotics should be used only for clinical indications/orders.
teaching: Avoid traction and report sudden leakage, pain, fever, or tube displacement.
delegationScope: Routine site/output care may be delegated to trained staff; troubleshooting requires licensed review.
examTrap: Assuming a suprapubic catheter cannot cause CAUTI-type infection problems.
oneLinePearl: Different entry site, same need for drainage and infection vigilance.

title: Hematuria and Clot Retention: Drainage Can Fail Fast
bottomLine: Gross hematuria with clots can obstruct urinary drainage and cause painful retention. Increasing blood, falling output, bladder distention, or hemodynamic change requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Bright-red urine, clots, catheter bypassing, suprapubic pain, and decreased drainage suggest active bleeding or clot obstruction.
priorities: Assess hemodynamics and drainage, inspect tubing for clots/kinks, and notify the urologic team.
assessMonitor: Trend urine color/output, clots, HR/BP, pain, hemoglobin/labs as ordered, and anticoagulant exposure.
interventions: Use prescribed continuous bladder irrigation or manual irrigation only under the specific urologic protocol/order.
medicationSafety: Review anticoagulants/antiplatelets but do not independently stop therapy without direction unless emergency protocol applies.
teaching: Report worsening red urine, clots, dizziness, or catheter blockage promptly.
delegationScope: CBI/irrigation authority is policy- and competency-dependent.
examTrap: Increasing irrigation independently without confirming the prescribed urologic plan.
oneLinePearl: Blood plus no drainage is a clot-retention emergency until proven otherwise.

title: Urine Culture From a Catheter: Sample the Port, Not the Bag
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: When a catheterized patient truly needs a urine culture, collect the specimen using the designated sampling port and aseptic technique according to policy—not from urine sitting in the collection bag.
recognize: Improper sampling increases contamination and can drive unnecessary antibiotics.
priorities: Confirm there is a clinical indication for culture, disinfect the sampling port, and collect using the approved method.
assessMonitor: Document symptoms, catheter duration, specimen method, and timing relative to catheter replacement when relevant.
interventions: Send the specimen promptly using laboratory handling requirements.
medicationSafety: Do not start or continue antibiotics solely because a poorly collected culture grows bacteria.
redFlags: Culture ordered for asymptomatic cloudy urine alone
teaching: Explain that catheterized urine often contains bacteria without true infection.
delegationScope: Specimen collection may be performed by trained staff per policy; indication and interpretation require licensed/provider judgment.
examTrap: Collecting the culture from the drainage bag because it is easier.
oneLinePearl: Culture the patient, not the bag.

title: Catheter Bacteriuria: Positive Culture Does Not Equal CAUTI
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Bacteriuria is common with urinary catheters. In most patients, a positive culture without compatible symptoms does not mean symptomatic CAUTI and should not automatically trigger antibiotics.
recognize: Cloudy or odorous urine alone is not sufficient evidence of symptomatic infection.
priorities: Assess for fever, flank/suprapubic pain, hemodynamic change, or other compatible symptoms and alternative causes.
assessMonitor: Review symptoms, vitals, catheter indication/duration, culture quality, and other infection sources.
interventions: Use urine-culture stewardship and remove unnecessary catheters.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria except specific guideline-defined circumstances managed by the clinical team.
redFlags: Treating culture results without assessing symptoms
Missing sepsis signs because urine is assumed to be the source
teaching: Bacteria in catheterized urine can occur without infection requiring treatment.
delegationScope: Interpretation and treatment decisions require provider/RN/pharmacy collaboration.
examTrap: Calling every positive catheter urine culture a UTI.
oneLinePearl: Positive urine is not the same as symptomatic infection.
sourceBasis: CDC catheter-associated urine culture stewardship guidance

title: After Catheter Removal: Watch for Retention, Not Just Incontinence
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Catheter removal reduces infection risk, but follow-up must confirm effective bladder emptying. Small frequent voids, discomfort, rising residuals, or inability to void can signal retention.
recognize: Overflow leakage can occur despite a full bladder and should not be mistaken for successful emptying.
priorities: Follow the facility post-removal voiding/bladder-scan protocol and escalate persistent retention.
assessMonitor: Track time to void, voided volume, symptoms, bladder scan when indicated, intake, and mobility.
interventions: Promote privacy, mobility, normal positioning, hydration if appropriate, and ordered intermittent catheterization when needed.
medicationSafety: Review medications that may contribute to retention without independently discontinuing them.
teaching: Report inability to urinate, increasing lower-abdominal pressure, or repeated small dribbles.
delegationScope: Voided volumes may be recorded by assistive staff; interpreting retention requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Assuming dribbling urine proves the bladder is emptying adequately.
oneLinePearl: After Foley removal, output matters—but emptying matters more.
